_comment: Ceilings for the Rust engine's criterion benches (crates/*/benches/**), read
by benchmarks/check_engine_bench.py and enforced by
.github/workflows/perf-engine.yml.
WHAT THIS CATCHES: order-of-magnitude regressions only. Each ceiling is 10x
the reference measurement below, so a case has to get ~10x slower to fail.
That is deliberate. Criterion numbers on shared CI runners vary by a factor
of 2-3 between runs and between runner generations, so a tight threshold
would flake constantly and a flaky blocking gate is worse than none. What a
10x ceiling does catch is the class of regression that actually hurts: a
compiled-evaluator cache that stopped caching (a hit becomes a full Cranelift
compile, ~1000x), an allocation added to a per-step loop, an accidental O(n^2)
in the integrate loop, a dropped fast path.
WHAT IT DOES NOT CATCH: the fine-grained kernel optimisations. On the
reference machine, losing FSAL stage reuse costs ~8-18% of an rk45 step,
losing interpreter dead-register elimination ~25% of an RHS evaluation on a
Jacobian-bearing tape, losing the SDIRK frozen-Jacobian reuse a few multiples
at most. Those are guarded by deterministic *counting* tests instead, which
cannot flake:
explicit::rk45::tests::fsal_reuse_saves_one_rhs_eval_per_continued_step
implicit::sdirk2::tests::frozen_jacobian_is_reused_across_substages_sharing_a_shift
interp::tests::rhs_live_mask_is_the_shared_reachable_from_pass
The benches quantify what those savings are worth; the tests are the gate.
REFERENCE MACHINE: the numbers in 'reference_ns' were measured on a developer
workstation (x86_64, Linux, release profile with lto=thin / codegen-units=1).
They are recorded for context only - nothing compares against them. Only
'ceiling_ns' is enforced.
UPDATING: regenerate with
cd crates && cargo bench --workspace
python benchmarks/check_engine_bench.py --update crates/target/criterion
and review the diff. A ceiling that moves DOWN is free; a ceiling that moves
UP needs a sentence in the PR saying why the case legitimately got slower.
